cases.quote: In addition to CJK Ideographs, ideographic characters (cl-19) also includes some handful of other symbols. The following is the list of all non-ideographic characters assigned to this character class. / 漢字等（cl-19）の文字クラスには，“CJK Ideographs”の他に，いくつかの記号類が含まれる．次は，この文字クラスに含まれる非漢字の文字・記号のリストである．
cases.rationale: U+0026 AMPERSAND is the first row of §A.19's table, and its Remarks cell is empty — as is every one of the 465 Remarks cells of this table, in both locales. cl-19 therefore states no frame (字幅), no writing direction and no role of its own, and a listing that qualifies nothing is a listing that describes an occurrence on any frame. The same key is listed a second time under §A.27 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」, and that qualification is the only thing separating the two listings. This occurrence declares the ideographic frame, which is not the frame §A.27 names, so cl-19 is what remains. §3.9.1 puts the width question first among the axes on which positioning differs, which is why an answer here is not reachable without reading the declared frame; 383 of cl-19's 464 keys are in exactly this position, so a classifier that answers from the code point alone is wrong on 83 per cent of the class.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19, first row, against §A.27's Remarks column (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists 0026 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」, and this occurrence declares the ideographic frame instead. Answering cl-27 for an ASCII code point regardless of frame is the failure §3.2.4's Note exists to prevent: it says in both locales that full-width, fixed-space Western characters are treated as members of cl-19, which is the reason §A.19 lists ASCII code points at all.

cases.quote: Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else? / 文字・記号の字幅は，全角か，半角か，又はそれ以外か．
cases.rationale: The same code point as the case above on the other frame, and the answer is a different class — which is what it means for classification to be a function of an occurrence rather than of a key. §A.27's row for 0026 carries the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence declares exactly that frame, so §A.27's sentence describes it and §A.19's unqualified row is what remains for every other frame. The two cases differ in the declared frame and the caller's measurement and in nothing else, and their expected classes differ, which is the assertion. The advance is the caller's measurement of a proportional glyph and is not what decides this (ADR 0002): the frame is declared, never inferred, and a proportional glyph exactly one em wide would be undecidable if it were.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.27's Remarks column for 0026 (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Answering from the fact that §A.19 lists 0026, without reading §A.27's qualification of the same key. §A.19 says nothing about width, so it does not contradict §A.27; a qualified listing and an unqualified one are not two claims about one occurrence, they are a claim about the qualified frame and a claim about the rest.

cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: §A.19's Character column prints ＆ against the UCS value 0026, and it does so for 68 of the table's 465 rows — every ASCII key from 0026 through 007C shows its FULLWIDTH compatibility glyph. The §A preamble Note quoted above is the sentence that licenses reading the two as one key: the appendix lists the ASCII code point, real Japanese text carries the compatibility counterpart. So an occurrence whose text is U+FF06 must reach the class §A.19 keys under 0026, and this case and the ideographic-frame case above must answer alike. The frame is declared full-em and agrees with what U+FF06 itself asserts; a caller who wrote U+FF06 and declared the proportional frame has stated two incompatible things, which is a diagnostic rather than a class. Only the Wide and Narrow decomposition mapping can be used for this: full compatibility folding would take U+2160 ROMAN NUMERAL ONE, a genuine §A.19 row, onto the letter I and lose it.

permitted.source: JLReq §A preamble Note, with §A.19's first row (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Folding U+FF06 onto 0026 and then reading §A.27's row for it. The fold is what recovers the key; it does not discard the frame the compatibility character itself asserts, and §A.27's qualification is "proportionally-spaced", which a FULLWIDTH AMPERSAND is not.

cases.quote: In this document, full-width and fixed-space Western characters and European numerals are treated as members of the ideographic characters (cl-19) class. / この文書では，全角のモノスペースの欧字及び全角のモノスペースのアラビア数字の文字クラスは，漢字等（cl-19）として扱う．
cases.rationale: This is the membership rule, and it is why §A.19 lists 0041 through 005A and 0061 through 007A at all. Both halves of §3.2.4's Note state it, neither conditions it on anything, and it is a statement about classes rather than about spacing. The same key is listed under §A.25 and §A.27, both with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」; the ideographic frame declared here satisfies neither, and §A.25's membership additionally requires the occurrence to be inside a unit symbol, which this stream declares no construct for. cl-19 is therefore the one candidate left standing, on two independent grounds. The class's English name is not a description of its contents: §A.19 also lists 49 Greek and 66 Cyrillic letters, and §3.9.2's own Note says JIS X 4051 calls this class "Japanese characters excluded from 1. to 12." / 「1.～12.以外の和字」.

permitted.source: JLReq §3.2.4 Note, with §A.19's row for 0041 (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Classifying a Western letter from its script rather than from its frame. §3.2.4's Note is stated unconditionally in both locales, and §A.27's own row for 0041 is qualified "proportionally-spaced", which this occurrence is not.

§A.25 names 0041 as a character that may appear inside a unit symbol (単位記号中の文字), and this stream declares no unit symbol. §A.25's row is also qualified "proportionally-spaced", so the frame excludes it a second time.

disagreements.implementation: CSS Text Level 3 and the Unicode line-breaking model browsers implement
disagreements.behavior: The Japanese-versus-Western distinction is taken from the code point's own Unicode properties — East_Asian_Width and Line_Break — so U+0041 is narrow, Western text under every condition, and U+FF21 is wide. There is no way for content to declare that a U+0041 has been set on a full-width monospaced frame, and consequently no way for it to be treated as an ideographic character. The two are different code points to the model and the same code point to JLReq.
disagreements.our_reading: §3.2.4's Note makes the frame decide and says so in both locales, and §A.19 lists the ASCII code points rather than their FULLWIDTH counterparts, with the §A preamble Note explaining that the compatibility characters are what real text carries. So the frame is a caller-supplied fact about the occurrence and the class follows it, which is the same reading under which this case and A.19/ampersand/compatibility-counterpart agree.

cases.quote: When full-width and fixed-width Western characters or European numerals are set in vertical writing mode as "quasi" Japanese characters, inter-character spacing between these characters and hiragana (cl-15), katakana (cl-16) or ideographic characters (cl-19) are set solid, similar to ordinary ideographic characters (cl-19) (see Figure 99). / 縦組で全角のモノスペースの欧字及び全角のモノスペースのアラビア数字を正常な向きで1字1字配置する場合は，一般の漢字と同様に前後に配置する平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）又は漢字等（cl-19）との字間をベタ組にして配置する（Figure 99）．
cases.rationale: The first half of the pair that asserts cl-19 has no direction-conditional membership. The trap is real and it is in this very section: §3.2.4's *body*, quoted above, opens on 縦組 / vertical writing mode, while §3.2.4's *Note* — the sentence that assigns the class — opens "In this document" / 「この文書では」 and names no writing mode in either locale. An implementation that reads the membership rule off the body makes a full-width A ideographic only in vertical composition. Nothing in §A.19 supplies a direction either: not one of its 465 rows carries a Remark at all, and no cl-19 key carries a writing-mode Remark under any of the other 24 Appendix A tables, where twelve keys elsewhere do. The expected answer here is byte-identical to the vertical case below and to A.19/latin-capital-a/full-width-monospaced-western-letter, which states no direction at all; the three differ only in `input.direction`.

permitted.source: JLReq §3.2.4 Note, which states no writing mode in either locale (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Reading §3.2.4's membership rule off the section body, which is conditioned on vertical writing mode, instead of off its Note, which is not. The body states a spacing rule for one direction; the Note states a class for the document.

cases.quote: In this document, full-width and fixed-space Western characters and European numerals are treated as members of the ideographic characters (cl-19) class. / この文書では，全角のモノスペースの欧字及び全角のモノスペースのアラビア数字の文字クラスは，漢字等（cl-19）として扱う．
cases.rationale: The second half of the pair, and the direction §3.2.4's body does name. Its expectation is byte-identical to the horizontal case above, which is the whole of the assertion: the class of a full-width Western letter is the same in both writing modes, so an implementation that answers cl-19 here and cl-27 there has imported the body's 縦組 condition into a rule that does not carry it. Recording the agreement is what makes the claim checkable — a single case in one direction could not distinguish an implementation that has the rule from one that has the condition too.

permitted.source: JLReq §3.2.4 Note, with §3.2.4's body naming this direction (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: In JIS X 4051, corresponding character class for ideographic characters (cl-19) is "Japanese characters excluded from 1. to 12.". / JIS X 4051の文字クラス名は，“1.～12.以外の和字”である．
cases.rationale: U+0391 GREEK CAPITAL LETTER ALPHA is a member of the class JLReq calls ideographic characters, and it is not an ideograph in any sense the word carries outside this document. §A.19 lists 49 Greek and 66 Cyrillic letters between 0391 and 04FF, and §3.9.2's Note quoted above names the class as JIS X 4051 does — everything Japanese that the first twelve classes did not take — which is a residue and not a script. A conformance case is worth publishing here precisely because an implementation that filters cl-19 by a script property, or by Unicode's Ideographic or Unified_Ideograph, drops every one of these 115 keys and reports nothing. The frame decides between the two listings as everywhere else: §A.27 qualifies 0391 "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence is on the ideographic frame.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's Greek run, against §A.27's Remarks column (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Deciding the class from the script rather than from the two listings and the declared frame. §A.19 lists 0391 with an empty Remarks cell and §A.27 lists it as proportionally-spaced; this occurrence is on the ideographic frame, so only the unqualified listing describes it.

cases.quote: In this document, full-width and fixed-space Western characters and European numerals are treated as members of the ideographic characters (cl-19) class. / この文書では，全角のモノスペースの欧字及び全角のモノスペースのアラビア数字の文字クラスは，漢字等（cl-19）として扱う．
cases.rationale: U+0030 DIGIT ZERO is named by three Appendix A tables, and the three are separated by two different axes at once. §A.24 lists it under grouped numerals (連数字中の文字) with the Remarks cell "half-width" / 「字幅は半角」, and §A.27 lists it under Western characters with "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」; §A.19's own row is unqualified, like every row of that table. This occurrence declares the ideographic frame, which is neither of the two qualified frames, and sits in no grouped numeral, which §A.24's membership additionally requires. So cl-19 survives on the frame axis alone and cl-24 fails on the construct axis as well. This is the reading §3.2.4's Note states directly for European numerals, and it is the one place in the class where a Remarks cell names a frame that is neither full nor proportional.

permitted.source: JLReq §3.2.4 Note and §A.19's row for 0030, against §A.24 and §A.27 (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.24 qualifies 0030 "half-width" / 「字幅は半角」 and this occurrence declares a full em, and cl-24 is a class an occurrence joins by being inside a grouped numeral (連数字) rather than by being a digit. A classifier that answers cl-24 for every European numeral has read the table as a list of code points and dropped both the Remarks column and the construct.
§A.27 qualifies 0030 "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」, which the declared full-em frame is not.

cases.quote: During layout processing, the issues mentioned in the previous section are addressed by grouping characters and symbols according to their characteristics, and handling them as character classes. / 組版処理を行う場合，前項で述べたような事項について，性格を同じにする文字・記号ごとにグループに分け，文字クラスとして管理する方法がある．
cases.rationale: U+3012 POSTAL MARK is one of the 81 cl-19 keys that no other Appendix A table names — the others include 203B ※, 2121 ℡, the Roman numerals 2160 to 217B, 3003 〃, 3006 〆, 3007 〇, 3013 〓, 309F ゟ, 30FF ヿ, 3231 ㈱, the circled katakana run 32D0 to 32FE, the era squares 337B to 337E, 33CD ㏍ and 4EDD 仝. On such a key there is only one listing to satisfy, so there is nothing for a frame to decide and the answer stands with the frame left unstated. That is the assertion: an implementation that demands a frame before it will classify has imported a requirement §3.1.2 states for five other classes, and cl-19 is not one of them. §A.19's Remarks cell for this row is empty in both locales like every other, so nothing about width is claimed anywhere; the Common name cell reads 郵便記号, and the Japanese half of the §A preamble Note — 「なお，“通用名称”は，JIS X 0213の“日本語通用名称（参考）”である．」, a sentence with no English counterpart — says that column is JIS X 0213's informative Japanese name and not a qualification.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's row for 3012, which no other Appendix A table names (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: Ⅻ | 216B | ROMAN NUMERAL TWELVE | ローマ数字12 | (published twice, consecutively)
cases.rationale: §A.19 publishes 465 data rows for 464 distinct keys: the row for U+216B is printed twice, character for character, immediately after the row for U+216A. It is the only key any of the 25 Appendix A tables lists twice, over 1687 rows, and it is recorded as `cl-19-duplicate-u216b` in spec/derived/defects.tsv. A published duplicate is a defect of the document and not a statement about the character, so the answer is the same as it would be if the row appeared once, and the count 465 is not this class's member count. The case is worth running because two plausible transcriptions fail it: one that keys on row ordinal rather than on the UCS column produces two members and cannot answer for either, and one that asserts distinctness while reading the table refuses to build its own class data at all. U+216B is also one of the 81 keys no other table names, so nothing else is in play here.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19, the rows for 216B (§3.9.2); the duplication is spec/derived/defects.tsv `cl-19-duplicate-u216b`

cases.quote: 仝 | 4EDD | CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-4EDD | 同上記号 — and §3.9.2's illustration of the class: 亜唖娃阿哀愛挨〃仝〆♂♀ etc. / など
cases.rationale: The last row of §A.19's table, and the row that makes the class's two halves overlap. §A.19's prose says the table lists the non-ideographic members, and U+4EDD is a CJK Unified Ideograph — it lies inside 4E00..9FFF, and its own UCS name says so. So "listed in §A.19" and "is a CJK Ideograph" are not disjoint sets: they intersect in exactly this one element out of 464 keys and 101,996 ideographic code points. Any implementation that builds cl-19 as a union of the two must not assume disjointness, and one that partitions rather than unions loses or double-counts this key. §3.9.2 groups it with the non-kanji examples in its own illustration, printing 〃仝〆 together after seven ordinary kanji, so the document itself reads it both ways. The answer is cl-19 either way, which is the point: the two derivations must agree, and this is the only key on which they can disagree.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's last row and §3.9.2's illustration of cl-19 (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: In addition to CJK Ideographs, ideographic characters (cl-19) also includes some handful of other symbols. The following is the list of all non-ideographic characters assigned to this character class. / 漢字等（cl-19）の文字クラスには，“CJK Ideographs”の他に，いくつかの記号類が含まれる．次は，この文字クラスに含まれる非漢字の文字・記号のリストである．
cases.rationale: The largest fact about this class is stated in one sentence of prose and in no table row: §A.19's list is the class's own complement, so every CJK Ideograph is a member without appearing in it. U+4E9C 亜 is the first character of §3.9.2's own illustration of cl-19 and is nowhere in §A.19's 465 rows. A conformance suite that exercised only the enumerated keys would test 464 members and miss around 101,996, which is why this case exists and why it is not decorative. The document does not define "CJK Ideographs", so an implementation must operationalize the term, and the operationalization is an interpretation an implementation should publish; U+4E9C is inside every candidate reading — the URO, Unified_Ideograph, the Ideographic property and ISO/IEC 10646 collection 285 alike — so this case is answerable without settling that question, and the disagreements it would expose belong on the code points where the readings differ.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's first sentence, with §3.9.2's illustration of cl-19 (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: In addition to CJK Ideographs, ideographic characters (cl-19) also includes some handful of other symbols. / 漢字等（cl-19）の文字クラスには，“CJK Ideographs”の他に，いくつかの記号類が含まれる．
cases.rationale: The differential twin of the case above, and the one that catches a classifier which derives cl-19 from the frame rather than from the document. §A.19's first sentence puts every CJK Ideograph in cl-19 with no qualification at all — no frame, no direction, no construct — so an ideograph is a member on whatever frame the caller declares, and no Appendix A table names 4E9C under any other class. The frame axis of §3.9.1 has nothing to separate here because there is only one listing to satisfy. That matters because the reading this project publishes for a code point in *no* table answers by frame, and would answer cl-27 for a proportionally-declared occurrence; an implementation that reached cl-19 for 亜 by way of the frame rather than by way of §A.19's sentence answers cl-27 here and cl-19 in the case above, and the pair says so.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's first sentence, which qualifies CJK Ideographs by nothing (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Answering by frame for a key the tables do name. §3.9.2 leaves the *unlisted* code point implementation-defined and §A.19 states the membership of every CJK Ideograph outright; the two are different questions, and an implementation that runs the frame fallback before the ideograph test conflates them.

cases.quote: 〆 | 3006 | IDEOGRAPHIC CLOSING MARK | しめ — 〇 | 3007 | IDEOGRAPHIC NUMBER ZERO | 漢数字ゼロ（レイ）
cases.rationale: Twenty-five Appendix A entries key on an ordered pair of code points, written <304B, 309A> in the tables, and cl-27 lists <02E5, 02E9> and <02E9, 02E5> as two distinct members — so an Appendix A key is a sequence and a longest-match scan over the tables is the only correct lookup. cl-19 contributes none of them: every one of its 465 UCS cells is a single four-hex-digit value, so a cl-19 item is always exactly one code point. This case is that assertion, and it makes it by being answerable at all. The two occurrences are consecutive rows of §A.19's table with nothing between them, and the second is the one asked about because that is the ordinal a spurious pair key rooted at 3006 would consume: an implementation holding one would match across both items and would have to refuse the stream, since the key would begin in one occurrence and end in the next.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19, the consecutive rows for 3006 and 3007 (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: However, there are some ambiguous cases, such as "エディター（editor）は……". In this case, English spelling is indicated using parentheses in a Japanese line of text. In this particular case, Japanese design is better.
cases.rationale: U+2194 LEFT RIGHT ARROW is listed by §A.17 and by §A.19, and both Remarks cells are empty — in both locales. It is the only key of cl-19's 464 that another unqualified class also names. Nothing in the document separates the two: the frame cannot, because neither listing states one; the role cannot, because neither states one; the construct cannot, because neither cl-17 nor cl-19 is a construct membership. This is the residual ambiguity §3.9.2 concedes rather than decides, and what it offers in its place is a preference about one worked example — Japanese design is "better" for a parenthesis inside Japanese text — which names no class and is not a rule. Both surviving readings are therefore recorded with the choice that selects each. This project's own reading is the lowest-numbered survivor, published in docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md, which answers cl-17 here; the other survivor is cl-19, and an implementation is scored against the reading it declares rather than against ours.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md), the lowest-numbered survivor
The other survivor of §A.17 and §A.19, preferring the later class

cases.quote: ↔ | 2194 | LEFT RIGHT ARROW | 同等 | proportionally-spaced / プロポーショナル
cases.rationale: The same key on the proportional frame, where the document does decide. U+2194 is named a third time, by §A.27, and that row alone carries a Remarks cell: "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」. An occurrence declaring that frame satisfies the one qualified listing of the three, and the two unqualified listings — §A.17's and §A.19's — describe what is left for every other frame. So the ambiguity of the case above is not a property of the code point but of the occurrence, and declaring a frame ends it. That is why an implementation must report a candidate set rather than a class when the facts do not separate the survivors: the same key answers three different ways and only the caller knows which occurrence they have.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.27's Remarks column for 2194 (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Answering from §A.19's listing without reading §A.27's qualification of the same key. §A.19 states nothing about width, so it makes no claim about a proportionally-set occurrence and does not compete with the row that does.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: U+2195 UP DOWN ARROW sits between two rows of §A.19 — 2194 is listed and so is 2196, and the row between them is absent — and it is in no Appendix A table at all. That is not an exclusion and not a judgment about the arrow. §A's preamble bounds every one of its tables to the non-ideographic characters of ISO/IEC 10646 collections 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION", so a gap in the enumeration is a repertoire boundary; U+3004 〄 between 3003 〃 and 3006 〆, U+24EA between two listed runs, and U+216C to 216F between the Roman numerals are the same absence for the same reason. The sentence quoted above is what the document says instead, and it says the question is implementation-defined. So an answer here is a published reading and never a requirement, which is why this case's standing is unstated and both readings appear. On the ideographic frame the two agree; the case below is where they part, and recording the agreement is what makes the disagreement legible.

permitted.source: kumihan published reading (docs/decisions/unlisted-code-point.md), by frame
The unconditional reading: every unlisted occurrence is cl-19

forbidden.why: Adding an unlisted arrow to the class its listed neighbors are in. §A.19 and §A.17 both list 2194 and neither lists 2195, and §3.9.2 records that the handling of a character the lists do not mention is implementation-defined — not that the answer is the nearest table. A reading that extends an enumeration by adjacency would also have to decide which of the two classes 2194 is in, which the document does not.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: The same unlisted arrow set with a proportional font, which is where the two readings of §3.9.2's silence differ and therefore where both have to be published. The by-frame reading extends the one distinction the document itself draws over text its tables do not enumerate — §3.2.4 treats full-width, fixed-space Western characters as cl-19 and §3.2.6 gives proportionally set Western text the composition rules of cl-27 — and the frame is the fact an unlisted occurrence still carries; it answers cl-27 here. The unconditional reading answers cl-19 on every frame, which makes cl-19 the disposal class for most of Unicode. Neither is stated by the document, so the case records both with the choice that selects each. This is the boundary of cl-19 in its most consequential form: the class that would absorb every unlisted code point under one reading absorbs none of them under the other, and 101,996 ideographs plus 464 keys is what it holds either way.

permitted.source: kumihan published reading (docs/decisions/unlisted-code-point.md), by frame
The unconditional reading: every unlisted occurrence is cl-19

cases.quote: If IDEOGRAPHIC ITERATION MARK "々" is allowed to appear at the line head or that of inline cutting note, the character shall be treated as a member of the ideographic character (cl-19) class. (For how it behaves in combination with other character classes, see the cells for ideographic characters (cl-19).)
cases.rationale: cl-19 is the target of this change, and the target side is worth its own case because of what it does to the class's own enumeration. U+3005 is not a CJK Ideograph — it is Unified_Ideograph=No — and it is not one of §A.19's 464 keys, so under the second of §B.2 note 14's three methods cl-19 acquires a member that neither of its two membership statements contains. That falsifies the English half of §A.19's prose, which calls its table "the list of all non-ideographic characters assigned to this character class"; the Japanese half asserts no such closure — it contains no すべて and no 全, and the Japanese heading calls the table's contents 例, examples — and the Japanese reading is the one the document's own §C.2 note 1 requires. Nothing in spec/derived records that divergence. The change is total rather than positional: §C.2 note 1 sends the reader to cl-19's cells "for how it behaves in combination with other character classes" and §E.2 note 1 repeats it for the expansion tables, so a relaxed 々 answers cl-19 anywhere in the stream, which is why this case declares no line. The occurrence sits after an ideograph because that is where 々 occurs, and its class is a property of the second occurrence alone.

permitted.source: JLReq §B.2 note 14, first method: the mark remains in iteration marks (cl-09)
§B.2 note 14, first method, stated as a declared choice
§B.2 note 14, second method; §C.2 note 1 and §E.2 note 1: treated as a member of ideographic characters (cl-19)
§B.2 note 14, third method, which changes only an occurrence placed at a line head or a warichu (割注) head

cases.quote: There is no line break opportunity between preceding grouped numerals (cl-24) and trailing postfixed abbreviations (cl-13). The alternative approach is to allow a line to break before trailing PERCENT SIGN "%", in which case PERCENT SIGN "%" shall be treated as a member of the ideographic character (cl-19) class.
cases.rationale: The second and less well known of the two changes that add a member to cl-19, and the reason §A.19's English claim of closure is falsified twice rather than once. U+0025 is listed by §A.13 with an empty Remarks cell and by §A.27 as "proportionally-spaced"; on the ideographic frame declared here cl-13 is the sole survivor, which is the default answer. §C.3's four levels are where the alternative is put in force: level 2, Loose (Magazines), names PERCENT SIGN "%" among the characters a line may break before or after even though Table 2 prohibits it — 「後置省略記号（cl-13）のパーセント[%] (PERCENT SIGN)」 — while level 3, Strict, the document's own default, does not. So a declared level of loose is exactly the condition the quoted sentence attaches its reclassification to. Whether the relaxation is a change of class at all is itself a choice: §C.3 states its levels as overrides of Table 2, and §C.2 note 9 states a change of class, and the two are not equivalent. The three entries below form a chain over those two questions, and only the middle one answers cl-19. §C.3 level 1, Very loose, relaxes cl-13 as a whole class rather than naming the percent sign, and this case does not assert what that does — see the report accompanying this file.

permitted.source: JLReq default (§C.3 level 3, Strict, which does not name PERCENT SIGN): §A.13's listing stands
§C.3 level 2, Loose (Magazines), with §C.2 note 9 and §E.2 note 8: treated as a member of ideographic characters (cl-19)
§C.3 read as an override of Table 2 alone, which permits the break and leaves the class where §A.13 puts it
